title: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co. (1950)
summary: Before a proceeding is accorded finality, due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties and give them a chance to object; publication sufficed for beneficiaries who could not be identified or located with due diligence, but known present beneficiaries with addresses on the trustee’s books were entitled at least to ordinary mail.
notes:
Distinguish adequate notice from personal jurisdiction. A state may have a legitimate relationship with a trust or its administration and still use a defective method of informing beneficiaries. Later cases address returned mail, known incapacity, and institutional delivery systems.

Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; Justice Burton dissented, arguing that supplemental notice for state-created common trust funds should be left to state discretion, and Justice Douglas took no part. Mullane was the court-appointed special guardian for beneficiaries who had not appeared, and it was he who objected that publication notice was constitutionally inadequate.

sections.Parties: Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company, a New York trust company, was trustee of a common trust fund and petitioned the Surrogate’s Court to settle its first account; in the Supreme Court it was an appellee. Mullane, the appellant, had been appointed special guardian and attorney for all persons, known or unknown, with a present or future interest in the fund’s income; Vaughan, also an appellee, represented those interested in principal. The beneficiaries themselves never appeared. The trustee sought a decree binding every beneficiary; Mullane objected that they had not received constitutionally adequate notice.
sections.Material Facts: New York Banking Law § 100-c let a trust company pool the assets of many small trusts into one investment fund; a decree settling the periodic account bound everyone with an interest in the fund and cut off claims against the trustee for mismanagement during the period. Central Hanover established its fund in January 1946 and petitioned in March 1947 to settle its first account; 113 trusts participated, about half inter vivos and half testamentary, with capital near three million dollars, and some beneficiaries lived outside New York. The only notice was the statutory one: publication in a local newspaper for four successive weeks giving the company’s name, the fund’s name and date and a list of participating trusts, naming no beneficiary. When each trust entered the fund the company had mailed known adult income beneficiaries a copy of the statute, months or years earlier.
sections.Procedural History: Mullane appeared specially and objected that the statutory notice was inadequate under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, so the Surrogate’s Court lacked jurisdiction to enter a binding decree. The Surrogate overruled the objections and entered a final decree accepting the account; the Appellate Division and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, holding the notice constitutionally sufficient. The case came to the Supreme Court on appeal, the route then available when a state’s highest court upheld a state statute against a federal constitutional challenge. Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; Justice Burton dissented; Justice Douglas took no part. The Court reversed and remanded on April 24, 1950.
sections.Issue: Could New York bind beneficiaries who lived outside the state and were never personally served, when the decree adjudicated their personal claims against the trustee rather than title to specific property? If so, was newspaper publication constitutionally adequate for each class of beneficiary: those whose interests or whereabouts could not be found with due diligence, those whose interests were conjectural or future, and known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had on its books?
sections.Holding: New York’s power did not depend on labeling the proceeding in rem, quasi in rem or in personam; its interest in closing trusts that exist by the grace of its laws and are administered under its courts’ supervision let it determine the interests of all claimants, resident or not, provided the procedure gave them a full opportunity to be heard. Due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to object. Publication sufficed for beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence and for conjectural or future interests; it failed for known present beneficiaries of known residence, who were entitled at least to ordinary mail. Personal service was not required.
sections.Reasoning: The Court declined to decide by classification: accounting proceedings had been called in rem, quasi in rem and in the nature of in rem, and the Fourteenth Amendment does not depend on a classification so elusive. Power gave way to opportunity: an adjudication that deprives a person of property must be preceded by notice and a hearing appropriate to the case, and when notice is a person’s due, process which is a mere gesture is not due process. The means chosen must be such as one desirous of actually informing the absentee might reasonably adopt: reasonably certain to inform, or, where that is impossible, not substantially less likely to succeed than feasible substitutes. Publication is a feint for known persons, since chance alone brings a back-page notice to a reader and this one named no beneficiary. For known beneficiaries with addresses on the trustee’s books, the mails were cheap and efficient, the class shared identical interests so notice to most protected all, and fiction should not deny the fair play secured only by close adhesion to fact.

sources.label: Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 1–5

learning.why: Publication alone was insufficient for known beneficiaries whose addresses were available, although it could suffice for interests that could not reasonably be identified.

topics.cp-notice: Notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to inform interested persons and allow objections. Known beneficiaries with usable addresses required mailed notice; unknown or unascertainable interests could be treated differently.
topics.cp-due-process: A proceeding that settles liability and affects property requires a meaningful chance to be heard.
topics.cp-class-notice: The later class-action notice cases use the same practical attention to identifiable persons and available methods.
topics.cp-hearing: Notice in Mullane matters because the accounting would cut off beneficiaries' rights, making notice the precondition to the opportunity to be heard.
topics.cp-property-jurisdiction: The Court refused to decide whether the accounting was in rem or in personam and held the notice requirement applies regardless, undercutting Pennoyer's category-based approach.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Burton dissented: common trusts exist only where the instruments creating the participating trusts permit them, and whether notice beyond the statutory publication and court-appointed representation should be required was a matter for the state’s discretion. Justice Douglas took no part.

mnemonic.rationale: Notice by newspaper to trust beneficiaries
